common_name: Ruffled Velvet Siberian Iris (Deep Reddish-Purple Ruffled Iris)

planting.note: Plant divisions a couple of inches deep in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; unlike bearded iris, Siberian iris rhizomes tolerate wetter soil and less frequent division over time.

directions: Plant divisions a couple of inches deep in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Ruffled Velvet carries richly ruffled, deep reddish-purple falls with a darker veining pattern, a more heavily textured, velvety flower form than the smoother petals of older Siberian iris cultivars, held over the same narrow, grass-like clumps of foliage typical of the species. Like other Siberian iris it tolerates wetter soil than bearded iris and shrugs off the rot and borer problems that plague its bearded relatives, making it a comparatively low-maintenance choice for a mixed border or pond edge. Clumps can go many years without needing division; when they do become crowded, dig and divide in early fall or right after spring bloom.

common_name: Sparkling Rose Siberian Iris (Rose-Pink Iris with White Signal)

planting.note: Plant divisions a couple of inches deep in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Sparkling Rose is one of relatively few Siberian iris cultivars bred with true pink tones, most of the class running toward blue, purple, and white.

directions: Plant divisions a couple of inches deep in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Sparkling Rose bears rose-pink falls brightened by a small white signal patch at the base of each petal, a comparatively rare true-pink tone among Siberian iris, which are more commonly bred in blue, purple, and white shades, held over narrow, grass-like foliage clumps. It shares the wet-soil tolerance and low disease pressure typical of Siberian iris, making it a reliable, easy-care choice for a pond edge or moist border where bearded iris would struggle. Clumps can go many years without needing division; when they do become crowded, dig and divide in early fall or right after spring bloom.

common_name: Great White Heron Japanese Iris (Large Pure White Iris)

planting.note: Plant divisions in consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to light partial shade; Japanese iris are heavier water users than Siberian or bearded iris and perform best at a pond margin or in a bog-like bed that never fully dries out during the growing season.

directions: Plant divisions in consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to light partial shade. Great White Heron produces exceptionally large, broad-petaled, pure white flowers characteristic of Japanese iris, flatter and showier than the more upright, narrower blooms of bearded or Siberian iris, on tall, elegant stems above sword-like foliage. Unlike most other iris types, Japanese iris demand consistently moist, acidic soil through the growing season and decline quickly if allowed to dry out, though they tolerate standing water for only brief periods rather than being true bog plants year-round; a pond margin or heavily irrigated bed suits them best. Divide clumps every three to four years in early fall to maintain vigor and bloom quality.

common_name: Plum Crazy Hardy Hibiscus (Dark Plum Foliage White-Flowered Perennial Hibiscus)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Plum Crazy's dark foliage color is most intense with full sun exposure and consistent moisture through the growing season.

directions: Plum Crazy pairs deep plum-purple, near-black foliage with enormous white, dinner-plate-sized flowers marked by a bold dark red-purple eye at the center, a striking contrast between dark leaves and pale bloom that stands out from the greener-leaved hardy hibiscus cultivars. Like other Hibiscus moscheutos selections it is naturally a wetland-edge plant and performs best in consistently moist, fertile soil in full sun, flowering from midsummer into fall on a robust, well-branched perennial. It dies back completely to the ground each winter and emerges quite late in spring, so mark its location to avoid disturbing the dormant crown, and expect it to be generally trouble-free once established given adequate water.

common_name: Jazzberry Jam Hardy Hibiscus (Fuchsia-Pink Compact Perennial Hibiscus)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Jazzberry Jam's compact, well-branched habit needs less staking than older, taller hardy hibiscus cultivars.

directions: Jazzberry Jam produces vivid fuchsia-pink, dinner-plate-sized flowers with a deeper red eye at the center, on a compact, sturdy, well-branched plant bred to stay shorter and less prone to flopping than older hardy hibiscus cultivars. Like other Hibiscus moscheutos selections it is naturally suited to wetland-edge conditions and needs consistently moist, fertile soil in full sun to bloom well from midsummer into fall. It dies back completely to the ground each winter and is slow to re-emerge in spring, so mark its location to avoid disturbing the dormant crown, and expect vigorous, trouble-free regrowth each year given adequate water and sun.
